🤖🎵
The Herdr explainer is already on the current skill **shape**: one question at a time, Reset/Randomize, Previous/Next, a progress bar, and the same font and Liatrio tokens. The gap is the **quiz shell**, not the teaching body.

I compared `/tmp/2026-08-22_herdr-practical-explainer.html` to `references/explainer-template.html` (the shell the skill actually ships). I have **not** changed the file.

## What already matches

- Same document chrome: favicon data URI, Space Grotesk, `:root` brand tokens, TOC, freeform `<article class="explainer-content">`, quiz mount, named JSON script.
- Same quiz markup skeleton: Reset, Randomize, Previous, Next, progress track, question region, stacked feedback region.
- Same offline font payload.
- Author slots are filled as intended: title, subtitle, metadata, TOC, Herdr-specific diagrams/cards, and 8 quiz questions. That content should stay.

## What is behind the current template

The template quiz runtime was updated after this explainer was generated. The file still has the **previous** one-question renderer.

1. **Score line**
   - File: `Correct: 0 · Incorrect: 0` plus an `incorrectCount` counter.
   - Current: `0 of 8 correct`, with `class="quiz-swap"` on both status lines.

2. **Status-line motion**
   - Current template crossfades progress and score in place (`swapText`, `.quiz-swap`, `--quiz-fade-out` 100ms, `--quiz-fade-in` 400ms) so the row does not resize.
   - The file writes `textContent` directly and has none of that CSS or JS.

3. **Enter/exit timing**
   - Current: outgoing fade is short; incoming wait uses `quiz-enter-delayed` so a first-time panel appears immediately and a replacement waits for the outgoing fade.
   - File: one 666ms duration for enter and exit; `beginFeedbackEnter` with `offsetHeight`; no delayed-enter class.

4. **Feedback styling**
   - Current: `#quiz-feedback-region .feedback[data-correct="true"|"false"]`.
   - File: still requires `data-visible="true"` for the colored border, and still carries unused leftovers: `.feedback`, `.feedback[data-correct="false"]`, `.quiz-complete` (nothing in the JS uses `.quiz-complete`).

5. **Answer locking and a11y**
   - Current: `lockAnswers()`; `aria-describedby` is set when the button is created; unselected buttons get `data-selected="false"` when locking from a stored answer.
   - File: `applyStoredResponse()` only marks the chosen button; `aria-describedby` is applied after the list is built.

6. **Quiz HTML details**
   - Current status nodes: `class="quiz-swap"` and placeholder `0 of 0 correct`.
   - File: no `quiz-swap`; placeholder `Correct: 0 · Incorrect: 0`.

## What I would not treat as drift

- The Herdr article, content-local `<style>` inside the article, TOC links, and quiz JSON. Those are the author-owned slots.
- `SKILL.md` still describes one-question-at-a-time as a future “iteration-two” idea, and still says Reset restores source order. The **template** already one-questions-at-a-time and both Reset and Randomize start a **fresh shuffled** run. For this file, the template is the convention to match.

## Planned update (when you say go)

Replace only the **shared shell**: quiz CSS tokens/rules, quiz section status markup, and the quiz `<script>` runtime. Leave title, body, content-local CSS, and quiz JSON alone.

That should make this file’s quiz behave like a newly generated explainer: `N of M correct`, in-place status crossfade, and the two-phase enter/exit timing.

# Liatrio Brand and Design-System Router

## When to Use

Use this skill when the user asks for any of the following:

- Liatrio-branded UI implementation, static HTML, documentation, decks, screenshots, or social/hero imagery.
- Brand audits, compliance reviews, accessibility checks, and corrective design-system recommendations.
- Logo, logomark, motif, preview, typography, color, spacing, component, or asset-selection decisions.
- Visual polish for existing artifacts that should match the current Liatrio design system.
- Resolving stale or conflicting Liatrio brand guidance in code, docs, slides, or generated assets.

## Core Facts

These seven hold for every Liatrio surface. Everything else, load on demand.

- Dark canvas `#1A1F23`; elevated cards and panels `#1E2327`.
- Primary Green `#24AE1D` is the hero color for key brand moments. On light surfaces treat it as a fill, not a text color: it measures 2.94:1 on white and fails AA at any size. On dark surfaces it is safe for text at 5.65:1. Two shipped surfaces break this rule — see the accessibility section in `references/liatrio-design-system.md`.
- Bright Green `#89DF00` is the highlight, used sparingly and never as a dominant fill.
- Space Grotesk is the only typeface. Hierarchy comes from size and weight, not family.
- Contrast floors: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and non-text UI.
- Sentence case for headlines, body, nav, and outline buttons. Uppercase only for tracked labels at 14px or smaller: eyebrows at `0.14em`, filled CTA labels and chips at `0.05em`.
- Brand CTAs are square. Only nav and in-app chrome buttons carry a radius, at 6px.

## Two Authoritative Sources

The live brand site and the local design system cover different ground. They are
complementary, not competing — check the one that owns the question.

**`https://www.liatrio.ai/brand-data.json` owns** the color palette (HEX, RGB, CMYK),
the typography specification, the logo and logomark inventory with file paths, and the
four published usage guidelines. Fetch it directly when a task needs exact values,
print-ready CMYK, the full logo inventory, or confirmation that the guideline has not
changed since the `2026-04-14` stamp this skill was written against. Do not copy its
contents into artifacts as if they were skill-local guidance.

**The local references own** everything the site does not publish: dark-first visual
posture, spacing and radius scales, motion and easing, hover/press/focus behavior,
component recipes, layering and motif rules, and voice and copy conventions. These
exist nowhere else.

Three narrower rules follow from that split:

- The site's Icons, Components, Spacing, and Social tabs are rendered from a hashed JS
  bundle with no stable URL, so they are recorded in `references/liatrio-brand-site.md`.
  That file explains how to reach the current bundle when exact parity matters.
- `liatrio.com` is dead as a source. Never fetch it and never cite it as canonical.
- If network access is unavailable, work from local references and assets and say
  plainly that live verification was not performed.

When a genuine conflict appears, name it explicitly rather than silently picking a side.

## Task-Mode Routing

Identify the request mode, then load only the references and assets that mode needs.

- `implementation`: direct UI/docs/style changes. Load `references/liatrio-design-system.md` and `references/liatrio-component-recipes.md` before choosing tokens, type, layout, and motifs.
- `audit`: compliance findings. Preserve the Brand Audit output contract below, cite the specific sources checked, and give proof for contrast, typography, source freshness, and asset choices.
- `design-system implementation`: a current Liatrio design-system surface. Space Grotesk, dark-first graphite surfaces, green signal accents, flat technical components, botanical and texture motifs, local preview recipes.
- `static/offline artifact`: a portable static file, screenshot, or helper output. Use bundled local fonts and assets; avoid remote runtime dependencies unless the user allows them.
- `deck`: slides or presentation guidance. Use curated deck assets when present, confirm logo and background fit, apply the same accessibility checks as UI work.
- `social/hero image`: visual or image direction. Check the four official banners listed in `references/liatrio-brand-site.md` before composing something new. Confirm dimensions and background brightness, pick the right logo variant, choose motifs deliberately rather than decoratively.

## Core Rules

### Typography

- Space Grotesk for everything: display, headlines, body, UI labels, table cells.
- Weights: 300 for large editorial quotes, 400 for body, 500 for buttons and eyebrows and table headers, 600 for H2/H3/display, 700 for H1 only.
- Use the bundled font at `assets/fonts/SpaceGrotesk-VariableFont_wght.ttf` for offline artifacts rather than calling Google Fonts.
- Reserve a monospace stack for code, version tags, and technical labels.
- liatrio.ai currently ships DM Sans for body text while its headings use Space Grotesk. The published guideline says Space Grotesk throughout, and the guideline governs. Treat DM Sans as expected when auditing liatrio.ai's own code and as a defect anywhere else.

### Colors and Visual Posture

- Dark-first: `#1A1F23` canvas, `#1E2327` elevated cards. Light surfaces (`#FFFFFF` / `#F8F9FA`) are for deliberate editorial breaks, print, and product screenshots.
- One expressive accent per surface. Primary Green for hero moments, Bright Green for highlights, Violet as the editorial counterpoint at most once per surface.
- Status colors are reserved and semantic: Lagoon `#00C1DB` for info, Hot Red `#E63946` for errors, Flame Orange `#F77F00` for warnings. Never decorative.
- Hairline borders before shadows on dark. Flat technical cards, structured grids, restrained shadows, green glow only for active brand moments.
- For the full palette with RGB and CMYK, fetch the live brand data rather than guessing.

### Logo, Asset, and Motif Usage

- Maintain clear space around the logo equal to the height of the `L` in `liatrio`.
- Never distort, rotate, recolor, or place logos on low-contrast backgrounds.
- Horizontal lockups are primary; stacked variants are secondary and only for square or near-square placements.
- The standard logomark must not sit on a green background. Use `logomark_Liatrio_background.svg` (the square variant) or a reverse variant instead.
- Pick logo variants by background brightness and state the exact asset path you used.
- Layer botanical and texture motifs over the dark base only when they support the content hierarchy.

### Copy and Accessibility

- Confident, technical, low-fluff copy in sentence case. Default to `we` for Liatrio and `you` or `your team` for the reader.
- No emoji and no exclamation marks in marketing or product UI copy unless the user explicitly asks for a different tone.
- Meet the contrast floors above. Do not rely on color alone for status; add text, icon, or structure.
- Provide alt text for logos, motifs, and meaningful imagery. Hide decorative textures from assistive tech.

## Output Contract

### Brand Audit Format

Use this exact structure for brand and design-system audits:

```markdown
## Brand Audit

- Scope: [screens/files/components reviewed]
- Compliant: [what matches Liatrio standards]
- Issues: [specific mismatches with source references]
- Fixes: [exact token, typography, layout, copy, and asset substitutions]
- Verification: [contrast/logo/background/type/source checks performed]
- Source Validation: [local references/assets checked and live liatrio.ai JSON checked or not checked]
```

## Workflow Checklist

Work top to bottom. The first three run before drafting, the rest before final output.

- [ ] Identify task mode: implementation, audit, design-system implementation, static/offline artifact, deck, or social/hero image.
- [ ] Confirm surface, background brightness, audience, dimensions, and offline/runtime constraints.
- [ ] Load only the targeted references and assets for that mode rather than reading everything.
- [ ] If exact values or freshness matter and network is allowed, fetch `https://www.liatrio.ai/brand-data.json`.
- [ ] Apply Space Grotesk throughout, at the weight the type scale assigns.
- [ ] Choose dark-first surfaces, Primary Green for key actions, Bright Green only as a signal highlight.
- [ ] Check button shape and casing against the two-language rule: square uppercase CTAs, 6px sentence-case chrome.
- [ ] Select logo, logomark, and motif assets by exact path and explain the choice.
- [ ] Verify contrast ratios, focus states, non-color-only semantics, and alt text.
- [ ] Check copy for technical tone, sentence case, no emoji, and no unnecessary exclamation marks.
- [ ] Compare the finished draft against the targeted reference, then state the exact tokens and asset paths used.
- [ ] State whether live brand data was fetched, and report any source conflicts or missing assets.

## References

- `references/liatrio-design-system.md` — visual posture, token roles, type scale, spacing, motion, copy rules.
- `references/liatrio-component-recipes.md` — implementation recipes for heroes, cards, buttons, chips, forms, dividers, and compositions.
- `references/liatrio-asset-index.md` — which bundled asset to use for which job, and what to avoid.
- `references/liatrio-brand-site.md` — the Lucide icon inventory, component variant surface, and site spacing tokens that the live JSON does not expose.
- `assets/colors_and_type.css` — local token CSS.
- `assets/logos/`, `assets/motifs/`, `assets/previews/`, `assets/fonts/` — curated local assets.
- `https://www.liatrio.ai/brand-data.json` — live canonical palette, typography, logo inventory, and usage guidelines.

This looks bounded, so I’ll give a short design in chat rather than a spec.

A sticky section bar is a better fit for these explainers than the current TOC card. The card is useful once, then it scrolls away; the rest of the page is long, and orientation is the thing you actually need while reading. Briefing/report artifacts already use this pattern for the same reason.

The current two-column “On this page” block also fights the page a bit: it sits between the hero and the teaching, uses a lot of vertical space for something you only glance at, and then disappears. A navbar that occupies that same slot, then pins to the top, keeps jump links available without turning the page into an app shell.

The real constraint is label length. This explainer’s sections are things like “Herdr vs. tmux and screen,” not “Overview.” A single-row nav will wrap or clip on a 1000px column, and a wrapped sticky bar can cover headings on a phone. The briefing template already learned that: sticky on desktop, wrap with complete labels, and if the wrapped bar eats the viewport, unstick it on mobile and keep a back-to-top control. Anchor jumps also need `scroll-padding-top` so headings don’t hide under the bar.

**Recommended shape**

1. Keep the large title/subtitle in normal document flow. Only the nav sticks.
2. Replace `nav.toc` with a horizontal chapter bar in the same place: sentence-case links, 6px chrome, same in-page `#` targets so the validator still checks them.
3. Include the quiz as the last item.
4. Desktop: wrap if needed, highlight the current section.
5. Narrow viewports: complete labels, no clipped text. If the bar is more than about two rows, make it static and add a compact back-to-top control.
6. No extra title chrome in the sticky bar. That would make the explainer feel like a dashboard.

I would not keep both a TOC card and a sticky nav. One navigation surface is enough.

One decision before a full implementation sketch:

1. **Wrap the links** (my pick) — full titles, may become two rows
2. **Shorter nav labels** — “Runtime,” “Layout,” “tmux” — full titles stay on the headings
3. **Desktop sticky, mobile “Jump to” menu** — safest on a 390px phone with 7 long names

    def test_sticky_nav_expands_to_full_width_then_restores(self) -> None:
        self.run_cli("resize", "1280", "720")
        state = self.evaluate_script(
            "const toc = document.querySelector('.toc');"
            "const article = document.querySelector('.explainer-content');"
            "if (document.documentElement.scrollHeight < window.innerHeight + 480) {"
            "article.style.minHeight = `${window.innerHeight}px`;"
            "}"
            "const rest = toc.getBoundingClientRect();"
            "document.querySelector('#quiz').scrollIntoView();"
            "await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 900));"
            "const pinned = toc.getBoundingClientRect();"
            "window.scrollTo(0, 0);"
            "await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 900));"
            "const restored = toc.getBoundingClientRect();"
            "return JSON.stringify({"
            "restStuck: document.documentElement.classList.contains('unused') || rest.top > 8,"
            "restClass: toc.classList.contains('is-stuck'),"
            "restWidth: rest.width,"
            "pinnedClass: toc.classList.contains('is-stuck'),"
            "pinnedWidth: pinned.width,"
            "pinnedLeft: pinned.left,"
            "pinnedTop: pinned.top,"
            "restoredClass: toc.classList.contains('is-stuck'),"
            "restoredWidth: restored.width,"
            "viewport: window.innerWidth"
            "});"
        )
        self.assertFalse(state["restClass"])
        self.assertLess(state["restWidth"], state["viewport"] - 40)
        self.assertTrue(state["pinnedClass"])
        self.assertLess(abs(state["pinnedWidth"] - state["viewport"]), 2)
        self.assertLess(abs(state["pinnedLeft"]), 2)
        self.assertLessEqual(state["pinnedTop"], 1)
        self.assertFalse(state["restoredClass"])
        self.assertAlmostEqual(state["restWidth"], state["restoredWidth"], delta=2)

You have access to tools through dynamic namespaces, e.g. MCP servers, using `GetDynamicTools` and `CallDynamicTool`.

## Dynamic Tool Discovery and Invocation

Use `GetDynamicTools` to discover tool schemas, then `CallDynamicTool` to invoke one tool. Aim to minimize round-trips: ideally one discovery call followed by one invocation.

If the user mentions a product or service represented by an available namespace, and the request likely depends on it, proactively inspect that namespace before answering. If you are unsure which namespace matches, search with a relevant pattern.

`GetDynamicTools` supports these modes:

1. `{"namespace":"<id>"}`: returns schemas and full descriptions for every tool in that namespace.
2. `{"namespace":"<id>","toolName":"<name>"}`: returns one tool schema with its full description.
3. `{"pattern":"<regex>"}`: searches namespace and tool names.
4. `{"namespace":"<id>","pattern":"<regex>"}`: searches tools within one namespace.
5. No arguments: returns the full catalog.

Pattern-search and catalog results shorten long descriptions, marked by a trailing "... [truncated]"; namespace and single-tool lookups always return the complete description.

Always inspect a tool's schema before invoking it with `CallDynamicTool`.

If the available dynamic tools do not fully support what the user asked you to do, complete the work you can with the current tool set. In your work summary, include what you were unable to do and why. Do not use browser automation to work around missing tools unless the user explicitly asks you to use the browser.

## NETDATA'S UNIQUE CAPABILITIES

### Real-Time Anomaly Detection
Netdata performs ML-based anomaly detection (k-means clustering) on every metric during data collection. Each sample includes its anomaly status from when it was originally collected.

**Critical: Anomaly Rate Interpretation**
- Low percentages often indicate major events, not noise
- Time window context is essential:
 • 1% over 1 hour = ~36 seconds of anomalies (minor)
 • 1% over 1 day = ~14 minutes of anomalies (moderate)
 • 1% over 1 week = ~2 hours of anomalies (potentially major incident)
- Anomalies may be concentrated in time, indicating real events
- Always query actual metrics to see anomaly distribution across data points
- The ML model detected these anomalies in real-time without future knowledge

## TOOL ARCHITECTURE AND PATTERNS

### Pattern Matching Rules
**Discovery tools** (list_metrics, list_nodes, list_running_alerts) support patterns on their PRIMARY data:
- `list_metrics`: patterns on metric names (e.g., 'system.*', '*nginx*')
- `list_nodes`: patterns on hostnames (e.g., '*web*', 'prod-*')
- Secondary parameters (nodes, metrics) require EXACT names only

**Query tools** (query_metrics, find_*_metrics) require EXACT names for ALL parameters:
- No patterns allowed - you must specify exact metric names
- Use discovery tools first to get exact names, then query

### Tool Combination Strategy
Tools are designed to work together. Use outputs from one tool as inputs to others:

**Example: Find nodes running specific services**
```
1. list_metrics (pattern: '*redis*') → get exact context names
2. list_nodes (metrics: ['redis.connections', 'redis.memory']) → get only nodes running redis
```

**Example: Investigate performance issues**
```
1. find_anomalous_metrics (timeframe) → identify problematic metrics
2. query_metrics (exact metric names from step 1) → see detailed data
3. find_correlated_metrics (same timeframe) → what changed significantly during this period
```

## INVESTIGATION METHODOLOGY

### Discovery Workflow
Follow the data trail using these interactive tools:

**For "What's available" questions:**
- `list_metrics`: Full-text search (use 'q' parameter) or pattern matching
- `list_nodes`: Search by hostname patterns or filter by exact metric names
- `get_metrics_details`: Get comprehensive information about specific metrics

**For incident investigation:**
- `find_anomalous_metrics`: Discover ML-detected anomalies in any timeframe
- `find_correlated_metrics`: Find metrics that changed significantly during a time period
 (compares against 4x previous baseline to score changes)
- `list_alert_transitions`: See how alerts changed state during incidents
- `query_metrics`: Get detailed time-series data with per-point anomaly information

**For current system state:**
- `execute_function`: Get live information (processes, connections, services)
- `list_raised_alerts`: See currently active alerts requiring attention

### Investigation Flow
1. **Start with discovery**: Use broad searches to identify relevant components
2. **Get exact names**: Convert patterns to exact metric/node names
3. **Query for details**: Use exact names in query tools for deep analysis
4. **Follow connections**: When data reveals related areas, investigate them
5. **Reach conclusions**: Stop when you have sufficient information to answer comprehensively

### Tool Response Patterns
- **Categorized responses**: When results exceed limits, tools group by category
 Use specific patterns (e.g., 'system.*') to get full details for categories
- **Error guidance**: Tools provide specific instructions when parameters are incorrect
- **Next steps**: Many responses include suggested follow-up actions
- **Batch execution**: Run multiple tools in parallel for efficiency

## PRACTICAL EXAMPLES

**Infrastructure discovery:**
```
User: "What databases are being monitored?"
1. list_metrics (q: "*mysql*|*postgres*|*redis*|*mongo*")
2. get_metrics_details for interesting database contexts
3. list_nodes (metrics: exact database context names) → nodes running databases
```

**Performance troubleshooting:**
```
User: "System was slow yesterday 2-4 PM"
1. find_anomalous_metrics (yesterday 14:00-16:00)
2. query_metrics (exact anomalous metric names) → see concentration patterns
3. find_correlated_metrics (same timeframe) → what changed significantly during this period
4. execute_function (if issues persist) → check current state
```

**Service-specific analysis:**
```
User: "How is nginx performing?"
1. list_metrics (q: "*nginx*") → get all nginx-related contexts
2. list_nodes (metrics: nginx contexts) → find nginx servers
3. query_metrics (nginx metrics, specific nodes) → analyze performance
4. list_running_alerts (metrics: nginx contexts) → check for issues
```

Remember: Netdata's per-second resolution and real-time anomaly detection provide unprecedented visibility into system behavior. Use tool combinations to build a complete picture from discovery through detailed analysis.

### Infrastructure-Wide Anomaly Correlation
For multi-node infrastructures, this single query reveals cascading anomalies across all nodes:

```
query_metrics(
 metric: "anomaly_detection.dimensions",
 dimensions: ["anomalous"],
 after: <timeframe>,
 before: <timeframe>,
 points: <based_on_duration>,
 time_group: "max",
 group_by: ["node"],
 aggregation: "max"
)
```

This returns the COUNT of dimensions (time-series) that were anomalous SIMULTANEOUSLY on each node.

The resulting time-series shows anomaly propagation patterns:
- **Simultaneous spikes across nodes** = External event (network outage, DNS, etc.)
- **Sequential spikes with delays** = Cascading failure showing dependencies
- **Isolated node spikes** = Node-specific issues

The time-series visualization immediately reveals which nodes were affected and in what order - critical for root cause analysis in distributed systems.

After identifying the cascade pattern, use find_anomalous_metrics on specific nodes/times for details." source="mcp" />

def test_toc_utility_row_reveals_back_to_top_only_while_pinned(self) -> None:
        self.run_cli("resize", "1280", "720")
        state = self.evaluate_script(
            "document.documentElement.style.scrollBehavior = 'auto';"
            "const article = document.querySelector('.explainer-content');"
            "if (document.documentElement.scrollHeight < window.innerHeight + 480) {"
            "article.style.minHeight = `${window.innerHeight}px`;"
            "}"
            "const toc = document.querySelector('.toc');"
            "const utility = document.querySelector('.toc-utility');"
            "const inner = document.querySelector('.toc-utility-inner');"
            "const topLink = document.querySelector('.toc-top');"
            "const firstChapter = document.querySelector('.toc ol a');"
            "const restStyle = getComputedStyle(utility);"
            "const rest = { visibility: restStyle.visibility, opacity: Number(restStyle.opacity) };"
            "document.querySelector('#quiz').scrollIntoView();"
            "await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 900));"
            "const pinnedStyle = getComputedStyle(utility);"
            "const tocBox = toc.getBoundingClientRect();"
            "const topBox = topLink.getBoundingClientRect();"
            "const chapters = [...document.querySelectorAll('.toc ol a')];"
            "const lastChapterBottom = Math.max(...chapters.map((link) => link.getBoundingClientRect().bottom));"
            "const scrolled = window.scrollY;"
            "topLink.click();"
            "await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1000));"
            "return JSON.stringify({"
            "rest,"
            "pinned: { visibility: pinnedStyle.visibility, opacity: Number(pinnedStyle.opacity) },"
            "isStuck: toc.classList.contains('is-stuck'),"
            "label: topLink.innerText.trim(),"
            "afterChapters: Boolean(firstChapter.compareDocumentPosition(topLink) & Node.DOCUMENT_POSITION_FOLLOWING),"
            "dividerWidth: Number.parseFloat(getComputedStyle(inner).borderTopWidth),"
            "rightAligned: tocBox.right - topBox.right,"
            "belowChapters: topBox.top >= lastChapterBottom,"
            "topMarker: document.body.id,"
            "topBefore: getComputedStyle(topLink, '::before').content,"
            "tocReset: getComputedStyle(toc).counterReset,"
            "chapterBefore: getComputedStyle(firstChapter, '::before').content,"
            "scrolled, restored: window.scrollY"
            "});"
        )
        self.assertEqual("hidden", state["rest"]["visibility"])
        self.assertEqual(0, state["rest"]["opacity"])
        self.assertTrue(state["isStuck"])
        self.assertEqual("visible", state["pinned"]["visibility"])
        self.assertEqual(1, state["pinned"]["opacity"])
        self.assertEqual("↑Back to top", state["label"].replace(" ", ""))
        self.assertTrue(state["afterChapters"])
        self.assertGreater(state["dividerWidth"], 0)
        self.assertLess(state["rightAligned"], 24)
        self.assertTrue(state["belowChapters"])
        self.assertEqual("top", state["topMarker"])
        self.assertIn(state["topBefore"], ("none", '""'))
        self.assertIn("chapter", state["tocReset"])
        self.assertIn("counter(chapter)", state["chapterBefore"])
        self.assertGreater(state["scrolled"], 40)
        self.assertLess(state["restored"], 20)

Moving the reset back onto `.toc ol` re-scopes it to the list. That was only safe once the list stopped being `display: contents`, which is why it lived on the nav until now.
